title: How To Handle Students Who Continue To Misbehave
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin identifies two root causes for persistent student misbehavior: ill-defined boundary lines and inconsistent enforcement. On boundaries, he argues that children of every age instinctively test for limits, and if none are found, misbehavior escalates and becomes progressively harder to reverse; the fix is exacting, highly detailed modeling and teaching of exactly what following and breaking each rule looks like. On enforcement, he argues that detailed rules are worthless without consistent follow-through, since inconsistency communicates that a teacher can't be trusted with anything, including instruction, and stems primarily from fear or favoritism rather than genuine leniency. He reframes persistent misbehavior as students unconsciously seeking the safety of a firm boundary, arguing that students are actually happier once a clear, enforced line exists, and closes with a directive to teach rules as if one's career depends on it and enforce them without wavering.
points: Persistent misbehavior stems from two causes: ill-defined boundaries and inconsistent enforcement.
Children instinctively test for boundaries; if none are found, misbehavior escalates and becomes harder to reverse over time.
Detailed rules are worthless without consistent enforcement, which he attributes mainly to teacher fear or favoritism.
Persistent testing of limits is reframed as students unconsciously seeking the safety of a firm, known boundary.
The prescribed fix is teaching rules with career-level seriousness and enforcing them without wavering.
quotes: There are two reasons why students continue to misbehave in the classroom.
By nature, children as young as one and all the way up until adulthood will push and test for boundaries until they find them.
This underscores the importance of ensuring that your students know precisely where your boundary lines are.

They want you to say no. Though they can’t always put it into words, or even understand their conflicted feelings, students are happy in a well-run and well-behaved classroom is because it means that someone cares.
Inconsistency tells students that you don’t mean what you say. It lets them know that you can’t be trusted with anything, academic instruction included.

To enforce consequences means that you can’t be afraid. Fear, and its close cousin, playing favorites, is the number one reason teachers look the other way or pretend they didn’t see what they just saw.
So, teach your rules like your career and peace of mind depend on it (they do) and do not waver an inch.
